content.text:
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Welcome everybody to BP's Q4 and Full Year Results Call. We'll be focusing today's call on the Q4 and 2024 performance and the contents of the video that I hope many of you will have seen by now. I also understand there is significant interest in our capital markets update in a couple of weeks' time. However, I'm sure you'll also appreciate that we can't comment on any issues relating to that today. Please focus your questions accordingly. With that, let me hand over to Murray.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Thanks, Craig, and thanks everyone for joining Kate and me on the call today. When I look back at 2024, we've achieved a lot. We've made significant strategic progress, taking decisive action and reshaping our portfolio and laying the foundations for growth, including 10 new FIDs, including Cascada and Tengiz, new access in Iraq and India, divesting tail assets in Trinidad, exiting the Empire Wind in the US offshore, decapitalizing our offshore wind business by agreeing to form a joint venture, JERA Nex bp, focusing our EV charging business and our hydrogen pipeline, acquiring full ownership of bp bioenergy and Lightsource bp, and recently announcing our intention to sell the Gelsenkirchen refinery. In two weeks time, we will build on the actions taken in the last 12 months and provide a comprehensive update at our capital markets event. It will be a fundamental reset of our strategy.
It will demonstrate our focus on actions to drive performance, and it will enable us to grow cash flow and returns and shareholder value. With that said, let me focus on today and briefly recap our highlights for this year. Many of our businesses performed well during 2024. Upstream production was around 2.36 million barrels per day, up 2% this year, with plant reliability above 95%. It was a good year for trading and its track record for delivering an average 4% uplift to Group ROACE now extends to the past five years, despite the lack of volatility. We have had a difficult year in refining with the Whiting outage in Q1 and the challenging margin environment. We were also impacted by the weaker biofuels margins and trucking recession impact on TA.
We remain firmly focused on taking action to improve our performance across refining and on the work to integrate our recently acquired businesses into BP, driving the synergies and underlying performance that we expect. Finally, on distributions, we grew our dividend per share by 10% and announced $7 billion of share buybacks, including a $1.75 billion announced today. With that summary, let's go to Q&A. Over to you to get us started, Craig.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Murray. Given my earlier remarks, I'm gonna ask you to each limit yourselves to one question so we can let everyone get a chance. We'll look to close the call by 1:45PM. There's obviously plenty of time in two weeks' time for more questions, and of course, the IR team is available to follow up. With that, let's get started. I think we will take the first question from Josh Stone at UBS, please. Josh.
Josh Stone
Analyst, UBS
Yeah. Hi, Craig, and good afternoon. Yeah, but with my one question, actually, I'll focus on the refining and trading performance this quarter. It was another weak quarter, but you talk about improvement plans. I just want to get a sense, how confident are you the issues you experienced in 2024 are now in the rearview mirror, and what more can be done to improve the profitability of that division? And maybe if you can give any early insights of how trading has performed during Q1, given we're almost halfway through. Thanks.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks, Josh. Thanks for the question. You're right, it was a challenging year for refining. The industry and the basins in which we are operating were probably bottom of cycle for margin and pricing. I think that's an industry-wide issue that we're a part of as well. Of course, we had the outage in Q1 in Whiting as well, an electrical fault that tripped the plant. In Q4 itself, reliability was fine across the portfolio. We, of course, had a massive turnaround at Whiting. It was a huge program. We replaced the coker tops, which is an incredible effort by the teams, and so that obviously dramatically impacted the results in Q4. As we look forward, we are confident that we will continue to improve the business.
Gordon can talk about this in a few weeks' time when we talk through what we're doing to improve the refining business. We're focused on four things. First of all, getting plant reliability back to that 96%, making sure that we don't have material trips. Turnarounds are going well, maintenance is going well, but we have to stick to it to make sure we hit that 96%. Gordon and the team are laser beam focused on that. Out of that then comes the ability to commercially optimize. When you have outages, you can't commercially optimize. We think between getting back to 96% and steady operations, that then lets us start to optimize and earn more money.
The third thing I'd say is there's a strong cost agenda across all of C&P, and that will really start to take root in refining in 2025. Last, we will have a year of much lower complexity TARS in 2025 than in 2024. That should all take us back to profitability. I think we feel confident in that. Again, in two weeks time, Gordon can take you through those plans. On trading, it was an average year, a 4% year, despite the lack of volatility on the oil and refined product side. I think you'll have seen some of that reported out of competitors about how far down they were.
The teams did well to make sure that we continued to hit that track record that we've had over the past five years. Now, looking forward, refining margins started the year very bad in January. They're starting to uptick now as we move into TARS season globally. I think the RMMs are up a bit, and we're starting to see some volatility. I think that's probably all I'll say, Josh, but we're laser beam focused on it. We know we need to do better, and we will. Thanks for the question.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Josh.
Josh Stone
Analyst, UBS
Thanks for coming, sorry. Thanks.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
We'll turn next to Peter Low at Redburn. Peter.
Peter Low
Partner and Co-head of Energy Research, Redburn
Hi. Thanks. Yeah. I just have a question on some of your upstream announcements. Your deal with ONGC and then also the redevelopment of Kirkuk. Can you perhaps talk a bit more about what you found attractive about those opportunities, and then potentially the sort of returns you might see for those sorts of technical service contract type agreements? Thanks.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep. Great, Peter. Thanks for the questions. Look, we've established a pretty strong track record in the Middle East and Far East to being able to help operators with late-life developments. As water starts to come into developments, as you have to develop tricky reservoirs, we've built a very, very strong reputation. Started in Alaska, moved to Samit. Rumaila is a good example of it, et cetera. We have a very strong track record in this, and that's what's enabling us to take advantage of these opportunities for direct access like in India and like in Iraq. In ONGC, it's a services contract. We're very pleased with it. We don't deploy cost or capital. Instead, we provide people and advice to drive stronger performance inside that business.
I can't really talk about what the commercial returns are, but they're quite attractive for India, and they're quite attractive for us. We found a nice middle ground where both sides actually can do very well for each other if we can start to drive that production higher. We believe, based on all the due diligence we've done, that we can certainly help India with that. On Kirkuk, we're in the final throes of the negotiations now. 5 domes of oil, 20 billion barrels yet to produce. A competitive PSA agreement, competitive internationally. Of course, it's because of our track record inside the nation that we're able to help them there. We'll give you more on Kirkuk once we've finished off the negotiations and announce it.
Let's see when the teams can get to completion on that. We feel very excited about that, and it will be internationally competitive, and we look forward to telling you more about that. Hopefully, at Capital Markets Day, we can update you more on that.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Peter.
Peter Low
Partner and Co-head of Energy Research, Redburn
Thanks.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
We'll take the next question from Biraj Borkhataria, RBC. Biraj?
Biraj Borkhataria
Managing Director, RBC
Hi. Thanks for taking my question. Firstly, thank you for the breakdown on the operating cost side, and it's good to see the sort of internal lens versus what we see. Just thinking about your strategies, it looks like you're gonna be including, you know, a more capital light approach, and, you know, more JVs and things like that, like the JERA deal. As it relates to your cost reduction targets, are you able to say the sort of quantum of costs that will, you know, come off your balance sheet as part of the transactions that have already been agreed? Just so I can get a sense of the magnitude of that. Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Kate?
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. Hi, Biraj. Thank you for the comment with regard to our cost disclosure. We have tried to help people by giving, I think, quite a lot more granularity and specificity than we have done previously. I'm pleased that that has worked for you so far, so let's see. With regards to the capital light approach on renewables, I think for capital, let's leave that to Capital Markets Day. We'll update you comprehensively with regard to capital right across the portfolio at that point. With regard to cash costs, we have already been successful in reducing some of our cash costs through focusing our portfolio, which we talked about on previous quarterly results calls.
It's part and parcel of the $750 million of structural reductions that we've delivered this year, which is great progress. Beyond that, we will just update you as we go. We will try and be as specific as we can quarter on quarter on the areas where we are delivering cost reductions and point out where they're coming from with regard to third-party supply chain or focusing the portfolio. We will make sure we give you enough granularity on that going forward, too.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Biraj. We'll take the next.
Biraj Borkhataria
Managing Director, RBC
Thanks.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thank you. We'll take the next question from Doug Leggate at Wolfe. Doug?
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe
Good morning, everyone. Or good afternoon over there. Thanks for taking my question. I guess it's like, it's a question for Kate. Kate, I wonder if you could just help us with the continued commentary around the $40 breakeven, but to help us benchmark the expectations for what you announced later this month. What I'm trying to understand specifically is you had this $917 million one-off cost, I think it was, this quarter. I'm trying to understand what that was, how that influences your view of where the run rate breakeven is currently. Excuse me, and whether the financing charges below the operating line are included in that definition. Just help us benchmark the starting point ahead of the Capital Markets Day. Thanks.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah, thanks, Doug. With regard to the balance point, we'll update the financial frame in totality in two weeks' time. The $40 balance point is important to us internally as we think about our dividend. It's a key part of ensuring that it's a resilient through-cycle. In terms of the one-offs, there were a couple of one-offs that we called out specifically in oil and gas. I don't recognize the 900. I recognize about a 400 that we highlighted in the O&P segment. There was 300 in there, which was associated with hedging and income from a sale of royalties and about 100 in the gas and low carbon. Really trying to be transparent and helping you as we move towards Q1.
I wanted to demonstrate there were a few things in our Q4 results that are unlikely to be repeated in the Q1. I'm happy that we sweep up after the call if you have a different number in your head.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yeah. Doug, the financing costs are inside the balance point, including the hybrid and interest expenses. That's all part of the balance point.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe
Thank you, guys. The 917 remeasurement of joint venture step acquisition is what I'm referring to.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Oh, thank you.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe
But I'll, um-
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah, I can tackle that one very quickly. The transactions that we had with regard to the acquisition of bp bioenergy and Lightsource bp were both step transactions, as we already own significant percentages of the equity in those organizations. It's just an accounting term. The $917 were both arising with regard to Lightsource bp. It's just a remeasurement of the existing equity we held in Lightsource bp and a remeasurement of the assets that we hold for sale in regard to Lightsource bp. It's a technical accounting non-cash.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Non-cash, yeah. Thanks, Kate.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe
Awesome. All right. Thanks so much. Appreciate it.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Doug. We'll take the next question from Alastair Syme at Citigroup. Al.
Alastair Syme
Global Head of Energy Research, Citi
Choose not to front run the strategy update, but you've put the words fundamental reset out there in today's press release. Can I ask what's gone on in the last few months in the environment and in your discussions with the board to change the emphasis from the prior wording that you used, which I think was mid-strategy update?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep. Thanks, Al. Nice to hear your voice. All I'd say is if you look back at the degree of activity we've had over the past 12 months, it's pretty significant. We have sanctioned 10 new projects, stopped 30 projects across the business. We've accessed new countries. We've completely decapitalized renewables. It's a sizable shift in the portfolio that we have moving forward. Given the degree of that change, it's now time to reset the strategy and plot a new beginning for us. It's just we've done an awful lot over the past 12 months, and this is the right time now to share that with you, the community. I'm excited to be sharing it with you in a couple weeks time. It's gonna be great.
Alastair Syme
Global Head of Energy Research, Citi
It's not the externalities of the macro environment, Murray?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
No. No.
Alastair Syme
Global Head of Energy Research, Citi
No. Okay. Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Al. We'll take the next question from Irene Himona at Bernstein. Irene.
Irene Himona
Senior Analyst, Bernstein
Thank you. Good afternoon. I had a question on your transitioning EBITDA. I presume this is the last time we will get EBITDA, given you're retiring the metric. I wanted to focus on bioenergy. It seems adjusted to the same definition that has remained flat at around $700 million a year. Can you give us a sense within that of the split between biofuels and biogas? The question is really about Archaea. Can we assume that Archaea has improved within that total since we know that biofuels margins were particularly weak, I mean, liquid biofuels? Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep. Great, Irene. Thanks. Archaea continues to improve, yes. Last year, we got nine out of the 15 plants online we wanted to. Three more are now online and functioning. We have three still flowing to midstream, but not yet able to declare startup. We've established 12 new plants this year, which obviously flow through earnings from 2024 into 2025. Certainly, we're seeing improvement in Archaea as we move forward. As you rightly point out, bioenergy is challenging. Sorry, biofuels are rightfully challenging. Especially in Europe, it's quite challenging. We don't see a lot of performance momentum inside biofuels in Europe. That's why we're being very, very careful with sanctioning any new plants. You may have seen a recycling in Australia as well.
We're pleased with progress on Archaea. We're not quite where we wanna be. We're probably 12 months behind progress on Archaea 'cause we had to take our time to make the designs work. We had to take our time to get the permitting right. We had to take our time to get the hookups to the midstream providers right. We've had to take a bit more time than we originally wanted to, and that's on us. With 13 plants up now, I think the closest competition is two or three a year right now, so we feel like we're in a good competitive position. Prices and demand remain very strong for it as well, and we'll look forward to continuing growth out of Archaea moving forward.
Carol will give you an update on that, in a couple weeks time, Irene. Thank you.
Irene Himona
Senior Analyst, Bernstein
Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Irene. We're gonna take the next question from Lydia Rainforth at Barclays. Lydia. Do we have you, Lydia? Okay.
Lydia Rainforth
Oil and Gas Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Yeah. Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Oh, sorry. Go ahead, yeah.
Lydia Rainforth
Oil and Gas Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Thanks, Craig. On the cost base, if I can come back to that, I think Biraj's words on it. It's actually a really helpful disclosure. You do talk, Kate, about the idea of a kind of strong cost margin ratio. I'm just wondering, is there any way you can sort of talk us through what you actually mean by that, how you measure it, and how that might have changed over the last couple of years? Because I think that cost base and it generating EBITDA is actually quite an important part for you.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. Thanks, Lydia. As we said in the disclosures, quite a lot of this variable cost, actually a huge part of it relates to our trading business. As you would imagine, it's a very, very margin-focused business. The analysis of that is just part of the way they work. We pay very close attention to the gross margin that we're generating on trading. If I look at what's gone on in the last few years, there's been about a 45% increase in shipping costs in trading as our freight rates are up. The other component part which you'll be familiar with is the scale of increase in our LNG portfolio. That's grown by over 50%. That's what's driving our cost base inside that part of the base.
In terms of variable costs, though, I think it's really important to understand that these are directly related to the delivery of margin. While we need to make sure that they are being efficiently managed, which we do, it would be crazy to put a target on those in terms of a reduction. I don't want to turn around to Carol and say, "Please, could you reduce your shipping costs?" That wouldn't be a great decision point in terms of driving value and returns as far as we're concerned. That's how we think about it, and that's why we've provided the level of granularity that we have and we will continue to provide with regard to our cost base.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
In a couple weeks' time, Carol will be talking about the trading business again, Lydia. She'll unpack some of this as well. I think you'll find that there's a fixed margin that we have across our business that's driven by this portfolio of shipping oil, of shipping diesel, bunkering, and the LNG expansion. More details to come in a couple weeks' time, and Carol will be happy to answer more detailed questions on that then.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Lydia. We'll take the next question from Lucas Herrmann at Exane BNP Paribas. Lucas, sorry.
Lucas Herrmann
Team Head and Research Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas
Yeah. Thanks very much, Craig. Hopefully you can hear me. Murray, I hope the op went well and that you're well. Very brief one. LNG and volumes this year, how much of an increment do you expect to receive from Beach, from Tortue potentially attaining volumes from Venture? Can you just give us an idea of the tons of increase that you're budgeting for? That's it. Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep, great. Thanks. Thank you for the kind wishes. I'm feeling great, Lucas. It's nice to be back in the office. Tortue and Beach are about 3 million tons per annum added, assuming a full year of flow. Venture, I'm just gonna not comment as the arbitration continues. Let's see how that arbitration goes. Hopefully, we see a ruling in the back half of the year on that, and then we start to see flow. I think between Tortue and Beach we've got 3 MTPA that'll come through.
Lucas Herrmann
Team Head and Research Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas
Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Lucas. Moving on to Matt Lofting at J.P. Morgan. Matt?
Matt Lofting
Oil and Gas Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Hi, all. Thanks for taking the questions. Two, if I could please. First, just on cost, I think you showed in slide 12, about $5 billion of structural cost reduction over the last few years. If I understood right, I think that includes divestments. I wondered if you could break down how much of that five is divestments versus underlying, given that BP's divested about $20 billion of assets over the course of that period. Then second, I just wanted to ask you about Russia and sort of Rosneft, given debate over recent days and weeks around Russia-Ukraine and sort of ceasefire scenarios, et cetera.
Could you see a sort of a feasible scenario and could it be sort of palatable for BP at board level around the case for reconsolidating the Rosneft shares in the future onto the balance sheet? I just wondered how you sort of see that today. Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Okay. Matt, you've broken the rule already, so, but we're gonna take that one. I'm gonna let Murray answer the question on Russia. Maybe first, Kate, on your costs question.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. We're not planning on breaking this down by portfolio movement, Matt. We're very clear that it does include portfolio, but we're trying to give you as much granularity as we can. I think we need to draw the line in some areas. Where it's a very big portfolio impact, of course, we'll try and call it out and help you with regard to understanding the underlying cost base going forward.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Lots of ins and outs in there as well. On Russia. Look, our principal focus right now is on divesting the stake. There are more than a dozen countries that have sanctions on the entity. We think the best focus that we can possibly have is on continuing to divest this, and we'll update the market as we go along on that. Thanks for the question.
Matt Lofting
Oil and Gas Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Sure. Thanks, all.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Matt. We're gonna just move to a quick question from Ahmed Ben Salem from ODDO BHF, who's online. Ahmed's question is, how do you see the impact of US tariffs on Canadian crude on Whiting's refining margins?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep. Thanks, Ahmed. Pretty difficult to predict is my answer. We have the ability to flow volume south to north in the United States if we need to. Obviously, the Canadian producers have optionality to flow some product to the West Coast and overseas as well. Upon announcement of the tariffs, the WTI WCS spread opened up quite a bit, probably absorbing half of that tariff. I think it's a very, very dynamic scenario, and it's very difficult to predict what will happen to margins on the northern tier. We'll just have to watch and see how the market turns out on this one. I don't think it's straightforward because there are so many different flows that get impacted with Mexican flows, with southern US to northern US flows, with Canadian flows.
I have studied it heavily with the teams, and I'm afraid I find it very, very difficult to predict what will happen. We will update you in due course as we learn about it. Thanks for the question.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Okay. Thanks, Ahmed. We're gonna turn to Christopher Kuplent at Bank of America. Chris.
Christopher Kuplent
Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you very much. It's, of course, dangerous to allow breaking the precedent. Let me try, and this could be a very short answer, but you may have your reasons for not publishing what the surplus cash flow is on a quarterly basis, but maybe you can just, yes or no, confirm that for the full year, it was somewhere around $4 billion. If I may, I just wanted to get an explanation how you feel about the value equation from issuing more hybrid bonds in November, which I guess will push up your cash outflows in the cash flow statement, which I make out at around 8% cost of that carrying value.
Just wanted to understand how attractive you think that is, continuing to issue hybrid bonds to lower your net debt. Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. We're gonna go back to focusing on one question. Kate, why don't you tackle the hybrid question, and Chris, we can follow up with you offline on the other question.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. You'll have heard me say in previous calls, Chris, I do think they're an important part of our capital structure. We're not seeking to build towers here. Just to be super clear, what we did in the Q4, which others also did, by the way, is take advantage of a really strong environment. The senior sub spreads were at an all-time low, and so we were able to issue hybrids in advance of our coming maturities in this year and in next year. It's really just a value play, right? The hybrid market can fluctuate. We wanted to make sure that when it was in a particularly strong moment, that we took absolute best advantage of that. That's all that's going on with hybrids.
I reminded that about half of our hybrids are fixed cost, and also that the payments with regard to it are fully tax-deductible. Yeah, I mean, they're not the cheapest, but it's an important part of our capital structure. We will continue to look very carefully and select maturities as and when the value feels right for us.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Kate. Thank you, Chris. We're going to turn to Roger Read in the US at Wells Fargo. Roger.
Roger Read
Senior Energy Analyst, Wells Fargo
Yeah, good morning or good afternoon to you. Let me ask a US question. BPX, just kind of an update on performance and how you're thinking about, you know, any particular increase in activity in any of the gas areas.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Hey, Roger. Nice to hear your voice. We continue to admire what BPX is doing. They continue to perform very well. We've got our third central gathering facility up online and full now in the Permian, and we're looking forward to getting the last one up around middle of this year. I think the most interesting bit we're seeing right now are these refracs inside the Eagle Ford, where the refracs and down spacing are actually creating more flow than the original mother bores. So there's something about a recharging reservoir going on there that we didn't really predict in shale. That's a very interesting opportunity as the returns are triple-digit plus on that space. On the gas side, we're contemplating increasing rigs right now.
Gas pricing is very, very solid as we look at the H2 of 2025 and into early 2026. Gordon and Kate and I are debating, should we be doing that? What head strategy would we have around it, and how many rigs should we grow? With the prices that we're seeing now, on the forward markets, the returns inside the gas now beat the returns inside the oil basins. That'll be something that we're thinking about, and we'll look forward to more questions in that space, in a couple weeks' time where you can ask Gordon about that stuff as well. Thanks, Roger.
Roger Read
Senior Energy Analyst, Wells Fargo
Thanks.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thank you, Roger. We'll turn to Alejandro Vigil at Santander next, please. Alejandro.
Alejandro Vigil
Head of European Integrated Energy Equity Research, Santander
Yes. Thank you for taking my question. My question is, basically about the slide number 16, of the presentation where you are
Talking about building momentum into 2025, and you saw this chart with a significant increase in year-on-year in EBITDA. Which are the moving parts of this increase? I imagine there are some consolidation portfolio, et cetera. I'm making this question also in the context of looking at consensus numbers, $37 billion for this year. Looks like there is a big gap between consensus and this is slide 16. You can elaborate on this, please.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah, thank you, Alejandro. Yeah. If you think about 2024 EBITDA, so we printed $38 billion for 2024. If you were to adjust that for 2023 prices, if you think back, I think it was Q2 earlier last year when we talked about the impact of price on our $46 to 49 billion EBITDA target. If you adjust our 2024 EBITDA back for 2023 prices, and if you think about 2023, although the commodities move around, taken as a basket, it's broadly comparable to our planning assumptions.
If you use rules of thumb, and you adjust for the fact that Whiting will be back up and operating well this year, if you adjust for portfolio and adjust for typical underlying growth that we expect to deliver year-on-year, you get to a number that's just under our target of 46 to 49, which is what we've said today. To be clear, we've said for a while now that our focus is very much shifting to cash. In two weeks time, we'll update you fully in terms of targets, metrics, and financial framework, and that will help put the retiring of this target into context for you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
I think on 2024 versus 2025, obviously, we've got the absence of the Whiting outage, depending on the margin, that's worth quite a bit of money. Then we have the 3% to 4% underlying growth that I've been talking about, quarter in and quarter out that we see year on year across the business. For 2024 versus 2025, that comes broadly across cost. Continued cost improvement, based on the great start we've done this year. Along with improvements in things like Castrol, TA doing better, European convenience doing better, Australian convenience doing better, and continued improved performance inside the upstream, along with, as I said in the refining coverage, less complicated TARS.
It's a lot of small things that add up to that 3% to 4% improvement in underlying plus the recovery from the Whiting outage in 2024.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Okay. Thanks, Alejandro.
Alejandro Vigil
Head of European Integrated Energy Equity Research, Santander
Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
We will turn to Michele Della Vigna, please, at Goldman Sachs. Michele.
Michele Della Vigna
Head of Natural Resources Research, Goldman Sachs
Thank you, and very much looking forward to the CMD. Just one modeling question from my side. We've seen two items before below EBIT which were larger than expected, the net interest cost and the minorities. I was just wondering if you could perhaps guide us on whether we should assume this is a new ongoing run rate or if there was any one-off impact in the quarter. Thank you.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. Thanks, Michele. In terms of net interest, that was up quarter-over-quarter, really just because our gross debt had grown. We took advantage this year in terms of markets and issued a fair amount of debt without actually buying back any more of our maturities. That's something that we'll continue to address as we have done previously based on value. In terms of the cash, it's a very minimal cost of carry right now, given the forward curves as well. That's all that's going on in net interest.
Michele Della Vigna
Head of Natural Resources Research, Goldman Sachs
Okay. Second for the minorities?
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
It's the, so there's a movement in, and that really just related to the change in hybrids in Q4.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
You would probably expect both to reverse over time.
Michele Della Vigna
Head of Natural Resources Research, Goldman Sachs
Understood. Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
You'd probably expect both to reverse over time as you decrease your hybrids again, and as you pay off your debt.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks, Kate. Thank you, Michele. We'll turn to Paul Cheng in the US at Scotiabank. Paul.
Paul Cheng
Stock Analyst, Scotiabank
Thank you. Good morning or good afternoon your time. Kate, can I go back into the 2025 EBITDA? You're saying that adjust for the pricing year will be slightly below the low end of the range. So comparing to the midpoint, that's probably, say, call it $2 billion less. Can you tell us that comparing to the initial expectation, which area that are seeing the miss and what's causing those? Thank you.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah, thank you. I think the two areas I would highlight, we've talked before about bio margins in Europe being suppressed, due to two reasons. One, the Nordic countries, rolling back their voluntary mandates to the EU mandated levels and also a level of oversupply from Asia. The other area I would call out is TravelCenters of America, where it's been slightly slower than we expected in terms of recovery from the trucking recession. We see green shoots. It's starting to improve. I think we're probably a year further out in terms of seeing full recovery. That's more likely to come through in 2026 now.
Paul Cheng
Stock Analyst, Scotiabank
Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thank you, Paul. It looks like just now the last question is from Giacomo Romeo at Jefferies. Giacomo.
Giacomo Romeo
Equity Analyst, Jefferies
Yes. Thank you. Just a quick one on the modeling side. Your lease has obviously gone up as you've guided. Just trying to get a better sense of where we should expect lease payments to move to going forward. In Q4, they were still relatively in line with the previous quarters. Just trying to understand whether they should go up and by to what extent into next year.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah, I'll take that. The leases were pretty flat quarter-on-quarter, but we did add to our lease liabilities in Q4 with the completion of Bunge. They've got about 300,000 hectares of land leased. So you will expect a small increase with regard to that. And then there was an extension of a lease that trading uses in the US, but for commercial reasons I wouldn't go into that. Q4 versus Q3, pretty flat, but you'll see a little bit of tick up with regard to the Bunge leases.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Super. Thanks, Kate. We're gonna let Biraj sneak in with the last question. Biraj, you've come back on, over to you, please.
Biraj Borkhataria
Managing Director, RBC
Hi there. Sorry. I assumed someone was gonna ask this, but, as I'm the last one, I might as well. Given the news yesterday around your new shareholders, any comments you can make about any engagements you've had with Elliott? Thank you.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Look, Biraj, it's market speculation right now, and we don't comment on market speculation. Thanks for the question.
Biraj Borkhataria
Managing Director, RBC
Okay. Thank you.
Craig Marshall
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, BP
Thanks for the question, Biraj. Okay, there's no more questions online, so we are going to close the call on that note. That's the last question. We'll close the call on behalf of Murray, Kate, myself, and also members of the leadership team who will join us on 26 February. We look forward to seeing many of you in London, and of course, those of you who will be joining the event by webcast. Look forward to seeing you in a couple of weeks, and thank you for listening in to today's call.

content.text:
Craig Marshall
Senior VP & Head of Investor Relations, BP
A warm welcome to everyone joining us in person at our headquarters today, and to those joining online and on the phones. I trust everyone has had a chance to watch the Q2 2024 video presentation and read our stock exchange announcement, both of which were posted this morning on our website, bp.com. We heard the feedback that you appreciated this new format. For today, we're aiming to finish the call at 2:00PM UK time. With that, let me hand over to Murray for some brief opening remarks.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks, Craig, and thanks to everyone for joining today. I'm in the room, and I'm joined by Kate Thomson, CFO, Carol Howle, EVP, Trading and Shipping, and Emma Delaney, EVP, Customers and Products. Which luckily for me, will provide me with the opportunity to pass all difficult questions to them today. To recap on today's results, our operations are running really well. 96% upstream plant reliability and 96% refining availability in the quarter. We generated strong operating cash flow of $8.1 billion. Net debt reduced by $1.4 billion to $22.6 billion. We remain confident in the opportunity and potential we have in growing the value of BP.
This should be clear with today's 10% increase in our announced dividends, the $1.75 billion buyback in respect of our Q2 results, and our commitment to announce $3.5 billion of share buybacks for H2 2024. That's $1.75 billion to be announced each at Q3 and Q4 results. You'll have heard from our video some real examples of us in action, delivering on our six priorities. We've accomplished an awful lot over the past six months. Of course, there's always more to do, and we have clear focus on our drive to 2025, which we can control. We see a lot of opportunity ahead of us, and we're remaining pragmatic, flexible, focused on value. We look forward to updating you on our medium-term plans in February next year.
Kate, Carol, Emma, and I are here to answer your questions. Can we ask each of you please to limit your questions to two? I'll go ahead and start off here in the room. Irene, why don't we start with you, please?
Irene Himona
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein
Thank you. Irene Himona at Bernstein, and congratulations. My first question concerns progress towards the $2 billion operating cost reduction target you announced, particularly in the context of a 4% increase in unit upstream costs, which I see. My second question on transition engine EBITDA, which in H1 has halved year-on-year. I can see biofuels, convenience, renewables; they're all down. So, it seems even if EV charging and hydrogen break even by year-end, the $3 to $4 billion next year looks a bit challenged. That was my question.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks, Irene. I'll let Kate lead off on cost, and maybe, Emma, you can amplify a bit, and then I'll tackle the TGEs and pass over to Carol and Emma as well. Go ahead, Kate.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. Thanks, Irene. As I said back in April at our Q1 results, we're aiming to deliver $2 billion, and I said then I'd like to exceed it. I'd like to be able to do it quicker. Since April, as you'd imagine, we've been in action right across the company in every business and every function underpinning that. The three things that are on my mind are, one, make sure that $2 billion is underpinned. Second, can we accelerate it? Can we deliver more? And then third, how do we make those savings sustainable? That's where we've been over the last three months. As you've seen today, we've now been able to get clear that we can deliver $500 million of that cash cost saving in 2025.
We'll continue to update as we go. Back to where I was in April, I would hope we can do better in terms of the delivery, but also the pace. Just in terms of the unit production cost, that's just portfolio mix at the moment. We're on track for the sort of around $6 that we said we would be by the middle of 2025.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Emma, anything to add on cost, please?
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Yeah, I think just amplify Kate, your point is the costs are owned by the businesses. We've run a process over the last few months, and the costs are embedded in our near-term plan for both 2024 and 2025, as well as that will flow into 2026. The majority of the costs are embedded right down into the business units, and there's some that we're still holding centrally. Murray, you talked about four buckets for cost portfolio. We're always churning the bottom of our portfolio tail end. You talked about digital. Just a couple of examples on digital. On cost. In my part of the business, we are, for example, rolling out self-serve checkout at our retail convenience site. That is a saving on labor cost, which increases, inflates every year. That's a sustained saving.
Things like our, on the digital side, we have multiple portals on B2B self-serve, which we're consolidating the back end so that you can still see a different front end. That also will deliver a cost saving as well as the ability to self-serve on digital. We're also in action. You talked about, in procurement, as a potential saving, Murray, earlier. Some of the things we're in action on there is in the US, for example, we are joining together our TA, ampm, TravelCenters of America, ampm, as well as our Thorntons merchandising. Now we have a bit more scale to go to market. Just some examples of how we're embedding and right down in the details on the cost side.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Fantastic. Thanks, Emma. On the TGEs, so last year we made around $1 billion of EBITDA. For H1 of this year, we made about $500 million. We've, of course, announced the acquisition of Bunge Bioenergia as well, which we expect to close in Q4. If you just pretend the run rate is the same, $500 million H1, $500 million H2, and you add Bunge Bioenergia into the mix, you're probably at almost $2 billion of EBITDA as a starting point headed into 2025. We remain on track to grow into the $3 billion to $4 billion range. We feel very comfortable with that. Emma, maybe you can talk about what we see in convenience and electrification, and Carol can talk about bio as well, please.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Sure.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Go for it, Emma.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Sure. I'll kick off. In terms of convenience and electrification, we're well on track to deliver around $1.5 billion from convenience and electrification together. EV charging lost zero with a loss of $0.3, so $300 million last year. We're talking about breaking even, so that will contribute to the $1.5 billion. In convenience, we're well on track. We did $500 million this year already. H1, that's up $200 million H1 versus H1. We're taking action both on the revenue line as well as on the cost line. On the revenue line, just a few examples. Our like-for-like sales are up and our store conversions.
When we convert stores to strategic convenience sites, which you'll see we've now increased another 50 over this recent reporting period. When we increase our strategic convenience stores, we see double-digit increase in sales just from those conversions. At the same time, we're working on our revenue line on the base business. For example, we're constantly innovating our offers. We launched pizza in Thorntons. That saw a 13% uplift in sales in the first month. We also launched just this year 13 SKU stock keeping units on water, which is one of the top-selling beverages for anybody who stops on the road, as well as sweet sort of jellies, candies. They're called Epic Brands. Why do I say that?
Because actually, consumers are under pressure, and consumers under pressure want a better value product, and we actually make a better margin from these private labels. Where we go directly to suppliers, conceive of a range of the top-selling products, it works for us, higher profit, and it works for the consumer 'cause its more value. I think as I put those together, we're now in the top five of convenience stores in the US, and our program in Europe is well underpinned with the pipeline of conversion, big conversions still happening in Poland. Here in the UK, we continue to convert at the margin, and then big program in Germany.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Thanks, Emma. Carol.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
EV.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
EV, I think you said we'd break even, and we feel comfortable with that right now.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Everything moving in the right direction.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Happy to come back to that after, if we like. Carol.
Carol Howle
EVP, Supply, Trading and Shipping, BP
Okay. I mean, I think first thing I'd say is on bio 'cause you did mention, bio. We recognize obviously globally in most markets it is weaker. I'll come to Archaea Energy shortly because that's one market where it isn't. I would say on the bio side, you know, we have seen lower transport tickets in Europe. We have also seen short-term oversupply. We've also seen some reduction in mandates, for example, Sweden, Finland. You know, there is some regulatory uncertainty which has contributed to that. We do also forecast that we're going to see margins improving through the end of 2025 and into 2026.
That's as we see mandates increasing in key markets like Germany and Netherlands, and that's also as potentially there might be import duties placed onto biodiesel into Europe, and also bioenergy is still needed to decarbonize the hard-to-abate sectors such as transport. I think Emma can talk to the business side of that more so. But I'd say there's a recognition, but we do still see positive margins for the future. In Archaea Energy, as I say, this a slightly different story. D3 RINs are actually holding up very well at the moment. It's a combination of high mandates, it's a combination of low availability around cellulosic ethanol. It's also the waiver credit there has been discontinued. I guess aligned with that on the basis that the margin environment looks as though it will be tougher going forward. You've talked in the past about margin shifting from Emma's businesses to refining business. How much of that would you expect may shift back? That's one question. The second, when you stood up at the start of 2023, you talked about the allocation of $60 billion or so of capital towards the transition growth engines over the period to 2030. I know you're gonna update in next year.
Do you still think that it's or $25 billion to $30 billion of that was gonna be allocated towards hydrogen, solar, offshore wind power in effect? Is that still a realistic number, or is that something that you really think you can allocate elsewhere or not allocate at all? That's it.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks, Lucas. Emma, do you wanna tackle the refining and margin shift question, and I'll tackle the second one?
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Yeah, sure. Thanks, Lucas. On the refining side, the first thing I'd point to is safe operational performance. That's always our focus in refining. This quarter, we had an availability of 96.4%, and four of our refineries were up at 96.5%. Just as a reminder, last year, the full year performance for refining was 96.1%, and that was a record since 2005, if I remember right. For job number one is to run the kit safely, and then we optimize commercially. Actually, we don't report refining, as you know, because we put it in products. We work very closely together with Carol's business on the oil trading and the product side and the midstream.
After job number one, which is safe operation performance, job number two is to optimize the commercial value. We do see value move up and down the chain from customers to products and back. I think as I reflect on 2022 and 2023, we saw elevated refining margins compared to history. I think 27 RMM in the 2022-2023 versus 15 in the period 2015 to 2021, if I remember. I'm not gonna guide to the future because, you know, it's really difficult. But we do with our trading statements, and Kate, you know, we do aim to guide as we go into each quarter 'cause the volatility just has been really, really significant over the past quarters.
In this particular quarter, Q2 2024, what we did see was our RMM is based on the typical configuration of refineries in a specific region, and then we blend it all together. Actually, our advantaged refinery configuration has more distillate weighting, about 60%. That's why you saw in this quarter, with the diesel, well, the distillate in general, but the diesel margin declined significantly with gasoline going up. That did impact our refining financial delivery this quarter. I think hard to say for the future.
Lucas Herrmann
Head of Oil & Gas Equity Research, Exane BNP Paribas
The occupancy numbers are great. What I'm slightly uncertain of is how much or the extent to which the kit is actually available and how much more kit is gonna be available to, you know, optimize, make money from, et cetera, in 2025 relative to, you know, the past two years. It's the scale of the TAs. I guess associated with TAs, I presume the costs of a TA actually are capitalized rather than taken through P&L. Is that correct?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yep.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Yeah. In terms of the TARs, we do give guidance on the TARs, and this year we've said that the TARs will be weighted towards H2 and Q4. I think on the portfolio side, you know, we have been streamlining our portfolio for some time now. With the six refineries remaining, we also have talked about in Gelsenkirchen in particular, that we will be reducing capacity from 25 in a controlled manner by about a third. I think from a throughput capacity and availability, I'm happy to pick this up later, but I think we give quite enough on the availability quarter-on-quarter.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yeah. I'll just go back to something, some comments we made in a previous quarter, Lucas, which is we expect the refining TARs to decrease in intensity from 2025 onwards because we've had a heavy dose of TARs in 2022, 2023, 2024 as we caught up from the COVID time period where it was impossible to mobilize individuals. We do see a lessening of the TAR environment from 2025 as we've done that catch up. Capacity, I think you can see the capacity. You can see where we're operating at. How much we actually utilize then is a question of supply and demand for the product. Right now, diesel is slightly oversupplied. Gasoline's about average. Let's see what happens in driving season. Generally, you deplete these stocks as we move through driving season.
The interesting things to watch are we have not seen any weather events yet in North America or Europe that would impact the refineries. We have seen them in Asia and the Middle East, but not yet in the West. That will play on forward margin and what the earning capacity is. There have been 600 KBD of announced shutdowns that have not occurred yet, from the third-party market. In Europe, UK, and the US, we should see that 80 million a day capacity shrink again as these things shut down, which again means less product flow and more chance for margin. I think my overall conclusion in this space, Lucas, is that capacity's tight.
Capacity is tight 'cause oil demand continues to grow, refining capacity in the West continues to shrink, and we continue to have weather events that are quite volatile. I think what that leads me to is we'll see quite a bit of volatility in margins around refining as far as the eye can see. That's how I relate to it, and that our earnings capacity will be based on how we do in that. On your capital allocation question, it's probably more a question for February than it is today. I think the statements that I can make right now are in offshore wind, we're happy with our portfolio. We're busy building out 10 GW. We will do that for as little capital as possible.
This, for us, is all about the electrons, so we'll lever these up as much as we can. We'll bring partners in, and this is all about electron flows into our own business. That's how we relate to offshore wind. Lightsource bp, of which we're buying 50%, once that's brought into the envelope, we adjusted a bit on what it's working on, and we are happy that we optimized it. We'll consider bringing in partners for that quite quickly. So that will mean there's very little capital intensity in Lightsource bp for us. Hydrogen, let's see how we get on the five to 10 plants. We've sanctioned two things, Castellón and Lingen. We have big decisions coming on Net Zero Teesside here in the UK.
On the Kwinana Integrated Energy Hub in Kwinana in Australia is a big decision, and we have a few more as well that we need to think our way through. Whatever those capital decisions are, that will determine what the capital is for the decade, and I'd hate to prejudge that right now. Hope that helps, Lucas. Another question in the room, Martijn.
Martijn Rats
Managing Director and Global Oil Strategist, Morgan Stanley
Yeah. Hi, hello, it's Martijn Rats, Morgan Stanley. I've got two questions, if I may. First of all, in the previous call, there was a question about the production profile in the H2 of the decade through towards 2030, and what that could look like. I remember you mentioning at the time said, "Well, we have 32 possible FIDs ahead, and what we decide on those will determine how that looks like." I fully recognize you haven't done all 32 by now, but you've done 12. And you seem to have some strong ideas about Tiber and a few others. Perhaps some clarity is emerging of what the production profile could look like in the second half of the decade.
You know, not to pre-empt yet another question that is shifted to February, but could you say something about the production profile in the second half of the decade? The other one I wanted to ask you is about impairments. BP is not alone in this, but the impairments continue to run at very high levels. Every quarter we go, "Huh, non-cash." But it was cash once. Impairments, you know, they're not, you know, they're not great. Can you say anything about what the outlook is for further impairment charges over the quarters and possibly years ahead?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Kate, I'll let you do impairments. On production profile, Martijn, I think we've gone through 12 different sanctions. Five of them we've approved, seven we have not. The two that we've approved in the Upstream, actually three in the Upstream, sorry. We did Atlantis DC1 last time around. We've done Ruwais, and we've done Kaskida. Tiber looks hopeful, but we need to work our way through the supply chain to make sure that's the case. I can't prejudge Tiber, but I feel optimistic about it today. We have done some, but there's an awful lot more to go as we think about it in that program of 32. I'm not really thinking about production. What I'm thinking about is cash flow and returns.
How can I really drive the Upstream to be as prolific as possible on cash flow growth through the decade at the return hurdles that we have or better? That's what that's how I really think about it and what we've guided on. Cash flow is growing to $25 and then relatively stable. I'm optimistic we'll do better than that. I don't know what the production associated with that will be, but I'm optimistic that we can do better with that given the quality of the portfolio. So let's see, Martijn. I think that's all I can say right now. Yes, we'll update you in February. Kate Thomson, over to you on impairments.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yes. At Q2, a chunk of the impairments were due to refining. We've made previous announcements with regard to how we're seeking to optimize the Gelsenkirchen and in particular, reducing the capacity there by a third. We said in the trading statement it would be $1 billion to $2 billion post-tax. We're bang in the middle of that. Impairments came in at $1.5 billion. The other point to just comment on with regard to refining is we, as a function of the accounting rules which push you to be prudent, we took onerous contract provisions in Q2. Those are calculated at a point in time before you have any option to commercially negotiate the outcome. I would expect we'll do an awful lot better than that.
I give Emma a stretch target now that we see that entirely reversing as we step through it, 'cause it's currently non-cash cost. That truly is non-cash cost. With regard to impairments going forward, it's a function of business decisions that we make and plans and environment. I'm not gonna start predicting what that's going to look like, but I take your point.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
It's a bit tricky with IFRS. It effectively brings your asset values. It just mechanically brings your asset values down to your price and your discount rate. If your discount rate increases, you impair. If your discount rate drops, you write back. If your price view points change up and down, you have to write back, et cetera. I tend to think of it more like advanced depreciation because it's forcing us to depreciate earlier than we otherwise might have, and it's the nature of the rules. That's just another thing to think about, Martijn, as you look at it. Next question in the room. Alastair.
Alastair Syme
Managing Director and Global Head of Energy Research, Citi
Hey, Chris. I just have a question for Emma about the marketing business. If you could give some picture on globally what you're seeing in same store sales, you know, particularly how maybe that shifts between or splits between footfall and basket size, and particularly within actually the US, given that you did call out in previous quarters you're seeing signs of consumer recession in the US.
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
In the marketing business, in terms of if I think about we've got, you know, we did $4.5 billion last year and aiming towards the $7 billion. There are four big areas of growth that we're aiming for. The first one is in continued performance and convenience. We saw 6% margin growth H1 this year versus H1 last year. To your question specifically on what the growth is made up of like for like versus store revamps, it depends on the market. In the US specifically, it's probably about a third like for like and two thirds store revamps. Each market is different depending on whether you have a program of store revamps.
For example, we have store revamps currently underway in Poland. There's more on the store revamp side. Continued performance and convenience will be a big part of our growth in the marketing businesses as we look through 2024 and 2025. In our base, you know, when I think about the base business, Castrol has now had six quarters of momentum. We had a record quarter in aviation this year, and our cost program that I talked about earlier will continue to give some ongoing growth to the base business. I talked as well about EV already and Bunge Bioenergia will also contribute in that.
As I look at sort of the big picture for the marketing business, I think we're well on track, and it's made up of a whole, I mean, literally 20,000 sites on the retail side. We work them top line, bottom line, and we work all the other B2B businesses as well. Really a big diverse portfolio there to get after.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Amazing. We're number five in convenience in the United States. Who'd have thought? Chris.
Christopher Kuplent
Managing Director and Head of European Energy Equity Research, Bank of America
Thank you. Christopher Kuplent from Bank of America. Two questions. First one is on your 2025 targets again, and I think, Emma, you refer to 2022-2023 as remarkable years, in many respects in terms of achieved refining margins. I wonder, can you add a little bit more subtlety around what I thought was a very subtle change already, suggesting that these EBITDA targets are to be achieved at 2023 prices. I recall that they used to be based on mid-cycle assumptions way back in 2021 when we didn't have RMMs above 20, and yet they were above 20 in both 2023 as well as in H1.
If I extrapolate H1 earnings, I kind of struggle to get to that EBITDA figure, even if I give you full credit for these EV and low carbon growth numbers coming through. I wonder what you can talk us through about that. I thought quite subtle change in underlying assumptions behind these 25 targets. Just a follow-up for you, Kate, on the network and capital. Is it appropriate to think about the Q2 as a roughly $1.5 billion reversal because the headline of $500 million or so includes the Gulf of Mexico spill payment? Are you confident that the remainder of the Q1 build is going to reverse in Q3 or what more color can you give us around that? Thank you.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Maybe if I take that one first. We had a $2.4 billion working capital build in Q1. It's about $1.5 billion that's come back this quarter. We've got about another $1 billion to come. As I said, I think earlier, we are expecting net working capital release in Q3. My expectation based on our current forecast is that net debt will trend down in Q3 prior to acquisitions that will consolidate acquired debt. Right? On the assumptions, I think at Q1, Murray, it might have been Q4, when we were talking, we made it very clear we were building from the 2023 delivery to how you get confident in the 2025 targets.
We said, "Okay, at these prices, with these buckets of growth that we've got line of sight to in the underlying business, that's how you get to your 46 to 49." We asked you to triangulate back to that. I think, and maybe Craig and the IR team can follow up afterwards. When the original slide was put out, there was a footnote at which talked about 2021 planning assumptions. Maybe, Craig, you can pick that up with Chris after the call.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Good. Yeah, Josh.
Joshua Stone
Executive Director and Head of European Energy Equity Research, UBS
Thanks. It's Josh Stone here from UBS. First I want to pick up on the decision to fully consolidate Bunge Bioenergia and Lightsource bp, because it seems like there are some companies in the sector choosing to separate out those businesses. You're gonna, you know, go out of your way to fully consolidate them back into the BP balance sheet too. Can you talk about, you know, the benefits of those businesses being part of BP versus a standalone entity? So that's the first question. Second one, I did wanna follow up on sort of surplus cash flow and buybacks, because if I look at H1 of the year, surplus cash flow has underperformed where your buyback level is.
You know, it looks like you've been using debt to help pay the buyback. But you know, when you decided to maintain the buyback flat and clearly using the outlook, and you've mentioned a lot of the positives of the outlook you're using to maintain that buyback. Maybe just go through some of the, what are the key building blocks in that improvement in surplus cash, and how much of an outlook are you using? Is it just the H2 of this year, or are you also counting on 2025 growth to help maintain the buyback? Thanks.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Sure. I'll start with Lightsource bp, then Emma, you wanna handle Bunge Bioenergia consolidation, and then Kate. I think on Lightsource bp, look, we had a partner, when we put it off balance sheet back in 2017. Fabulous entrepreneur helped us grow the business up to 4 GW or 5 GW development per year but hit the end of when they wanted to continue doing this. Now is the time where they wanted to cash out. It was convenient for us to go in and take control over the 100%. It's a fabulous vehicle to go and help Carol build out her business. So many customers around the world want natural gas coupled with power, clean power, to start to decarbonize their own energy systems.
With the growth of hyperscalers, we're seeing just increased demand after demand after demand. Taking 100% control of that entity, given that incredible native demand we see for energy, especially from the hyperscalers now and the desire of nations to transition makes an awful lot of sense. At the same time, once you've taken that control, you've restructured it, done some stuff to the portfolio based on where your customers sit, et cetera, you will then think about bringing a passive partner into this. You'll think about giving a passive partner it. They've got a very different cost of capital than we have. That should offer the chance to arbitrage the price over time.
Joshua Stone
Executive Director and Head of European Energy Equity Research, UBS
What's the timeline on that, Murray?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Well, let's see when we complete and then, probably over 12 to 18 months we'd bring somebody else in. That's why we think it was a really good time, both given where the partner was, the opportunity we see in the market, and how we see that business moving forward. That's how we think about Lightsource bp. Emma, on Bunge Bioenergia?
Emma Delaney
EVP, Customers and Products, BP
Yeah. I've sort of a very short answer on Bunge Bioenergia. We've been in the JV since 2019, so we actually understand the operational performance metrics now quite well and saw the opportunity to take the 50% to then consolidate to 100% because the two biggest sources of value are inaccessible to us as just a 50%. Namely, the first one is about integrating with Carol's business on the trading side. There's a big source of value there. Very difficult to do when you're 50/50. The other source of value is applying, Murray, you mentioned this earlier, some of the science, but also some of our techniques from refining on automated control systems, for example. We see the opportunity to increase the mill uptime.
Again, difficult to do when it's in a joint venture 50/50. I think the source of the value we can see them immediately ahead of us in the near term, and then there's tons to do long term. A lot to do on the biogas side. We can use the waste from the mills. It will take a relatively small investment, waste from the mills to be able to then convert into biogas, digest biogas, and then either use in our own net vehicle network. There's a massive vehicle network there. We have 1,500 vehicles, combine harvesters in the field, either to use our own fleet over time or to sell into the grid. That's a big opportunity. Again, hard to do when you're 50/50 and you have different objectives for the joint venture.
Then there's more to do in the future on next generation ethanol. I think those things we see both near-term sources of value and then in the medium to long-term opportunities for investment to really bring this to life.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Our decisions are driven by how do we create the maximum value for shareholders. That's how we drive, and that's the two examples in that case. Kate, over to you on the other question.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. When we updated the fin frame at Q4, we deliberately stepped away from the quarter-on-quarter calculation of surplus cash 'cause it was creating an awful lot of volatility and perhaps unhelpful focus on what's your absolute surplus cash in any one quarter. We wanted to provide predictability and a level of certainty into the market with regard to the forward share buyback. Q1, we had a Whiting outage that was significant, as you know. The surplus cash was lower than we might have expected. At Q2, the level of share buyback compared to surplus cash is down to 59%. What we're saying is 80% over time, at least 80% over time to surplus cash.
As the board makes its decisions, and as we had the conversation last week with regard to H2 2024, we take into consideration what's come today and what's coming forward. We're confident in the delivery of the business. We're confident in the improved performance. There's a lot of discipline that we're putting into the capital frame. As you know, we've tightened that right down to around $16 billion for the year, and we're bang on that at H1. Divestments are slightly higher than 2023 at $2 billion to $3 billion. We've probably got between $1 billion and $2 billion more to come on that. We've got a full year of cash flow from TA to take into consideration. We're confident in our delivery and our outlook for the remainder of 2024.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks, Kate. I realize that we're overrunning, so I'm gonna take one more call on the phone. Apologies for that, with Doug Leggate at Wolfe, and then I'm gonna have to close it down, and we'll follow up with any other questions out there. Doug, over to you.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you, Murray. Can you hear me okay?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Yeah, I hear you great. Thanks, Doug.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Bank of America
I'll try two quick ones, hopefully. I wanted to try and maybe circle back on the longer-term production outlook. A couple of quarters ago, you talked about 2 mmboe/d being the stabilized level. You're well above that, and you're now sanctioning new projects. I don't want to front run January or February when you report, but is 2 million still the right number?
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Okay. Did you have another question, Doug, or was that it?
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Bank of America
Yeah. My follow-up is I wanted to come back to the buyback question. I've had the pleasure of covering many of your peers for three decades, and the big difference between those buying back stock and yourselves is a much, much stronger balance sheet. If I look at your share performance since you started the buyback, you really haven't had any benefit. Your share price is down, and you bought back a fifth of your stock, but your net debt remains relatively high if you include the hybrids. I'm just curious why you believe that method of cash return is still the optimal way to maximize value for shareholders.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Okay, great. On long-term production. Yes, we're running about 2.3 mmboe/d right now, but of course we've got some divestments. We've announced the divestment of Egypt into a JV that will take effect in Q4, I think, which should drop production about 50 KBD. So, you'll be down at 2,250. Then we have some other divestments that we continue to pursue at low margin, high volume assets that may or may not happen, but if they were to happen, that would drop their production to around two'ish. As far as what the production outturn looks like for the back end of the decade, of course, we'll update you on February on where that is. I'll just repeat what I said earlier.
I'm focused on cash flow, and returns, and production will be an outcome of that, but I'm really focused on growing cash flow. If I just wanted to grow volume, I could plow all the money in the world into the Haynesville, and I could grow volumes like crazy, but that's not the right thing to do for shareholders. It's to create cash flow and returns. That's why I'm focused so much on that, Doug. I hope that helps you. Kate, over to you.
Kate Thomson
CFO, BP
Yeah. Thanks, Murray. Doug, hi. Nice to hear your voice. We've already had one debate with regard to share buybacks versus debt. I'm sure we'll have others by the sound of it. Look, I think I said earlier on the call, the investors that we talk to, they like the balance of the financial frame as we've currently got it structured. As I said, it's sector-leading distributions, and the balance sheet's in good shape. It is strong. We have brought it down a significant amount since 2020. The flywheel that the share buybacks give us to be able to continually increase dividends, as we've seen the last three years, have done 10% each of the Q2s. It creates a flywheel for that and the increasing Earnings Per Share.
For now, we're comfortable with where that sits, and we like the balance, and so do our investors.
Murray Auchincloss
CEO, BP
Great. Thanks very much, everybody. Thanks for listening. Sorry we overran a bit and hope everybody has a nice summer. Take care.
